body:
Sarah L.: Heads up — customer reported their ingress healthchecks start flapping after they add our egress allowlist & force all outbound through their corporate proxy.
Kevin M.: Oof. Any logs or symptom details?
Sarah L.: Short dump from their support ticket:
```
curl -v --proxy http://corp-proxy:8080 https://health.redwood.internal:8443/ready
* Connected to corp-proxy (10.10.10.5) port 8080
> GET /ready HTTP/1.1
> Host: health.redwood.internal:8443
< HTTP/1.1 502 Bad Gateway
```
They also say our LB health checks show up from a handful of internal IPs instead of the actual LB because the proxy rewrites source.
Priya R.: This is a classic NAT/proxy source-IP preservation problem. Two quick patterns we see customers do: allow our healthcheck source CIDRs on the firewall, OR configure the proxy to forward the original source (X-Forwarded-For / PROXY protocol) to the backend so readiness looks normal.
Anthony B.: Right — also depends on healthcheck type. If they use HTTP healthchecks through a corporate forward proxy, proxy will terminate and re-origin the request from its own IPs. TCP-level healthchecks that target the node IP:port generally bypass HTTP proxy behavior.
Kevin M.: Customer asked "what do we actually need to allow on their outbound firewall?" We should give a minimal checklist and one recommended approach.
Priya R.: Suggested checklist (short):
- For customers using an outbound HTTP proxy: allow CONNECT to our service FQDNs on the outbound proxy and ensure the proxy preserves/forwards x-forwarded-for or supports PROXY protocol when talking to our internal endpoints.
- For customers using egress allowlist only: add our documented healthcheck CIDR ranges (we provide per-region lists) to the allowed destinations so LB -> node healthchecks succeed.
- If proxy rewrites source and they cannot change it: prefer TCP (layer4) healthchecks or configure a dedicated internal health endpoint that accepts proxy-source IPs and uses header-based verification.
Kevin M.: Can we give an example firewall rule snippet they can paste?
Sarah L.: Example outbound rule for a corporate proxy (pseudo syntax):
```
# allow proxy to reach Redwood health endpoints
ALLOW tcp FROM 10.0.0.0/8 TO health.redwood.internal:8443
# allow the proxy to do CONNECT for TLS traffic
ALLOW tcp FROM 10.0.0.0/8 TO *.redwood-api.net:443
```
Anthony B.: And example iptables hack if they absolutely must exempt healthchecks from NAT on their proxy host (only for advanced ops):
```
# preserve source for node health probes (example)
iptables -t nat -I PREROUTING 1 -p tcp --dport 8443 -s 10.1.0.0/16 -j ACCEPT
```
Kevin M.: We should also call out common platform-level fixes: enable proxy-protocol on the LB and have backends accept it, or publish a small TCP health probe port that the proxy can allow through without HTTP rewrite.
Priya R.: Agreed. I'll draft a short customer-facing checklist and a section in the docs that explains: (a) proxy mode implications, (b) healthcheck CIDRs per region, (c) recommended TCP fallback.
infra-bot: NOTE: healthcheck CIDR list update pending — engineering will publish region CIDRs in docs by EOD.
Anthony B.: Action items: @Priya R. to draft docs, @Kevin M. to add a short ops troubleshooting checklist for support playbook, @Sarah L. to share the customer's proxy config.
Sarah L.: Dropping the proxy snippet from the customer (redacted):
```
# corp-proxy snippet
forward_mode on
preserve_client_ip off
```
Kevin M.: If preserve_client_ip is off they won't be able to rely on source allowlists. We should tell them explicitly: either flip preserve_client_ip on, or update firewall to allow healthcheck CIDRs and use TCP healthchecks.
Priya R.: I'll include a decision table in the doc: 1) preserve_client_ip=true -> allowlist unnecessary for healthchecks; 2) preserve_client_ip=false + proxy only -> need CIDRs or TCP healthchecks; 3) on-prem LB + NAT -> probably CIDRs and port exceptions.
Sarah L.: Thanks — keeping this thread for support handoff notes. :thumbsup:
